pages.headline: Convert record backlog into delivered work, not burnout.
pages.outcome: Your growth plan currently has one engine: hire licensed professionals fast enough to keep up with the backlog, in a market where every competitor is fishing the same pool. Governed AI adds a second engine. Assembly, drafting, retrieval, and synthesis move onto rails, licensed attention returns to design judgment, checking, and clients, and backlog converts to revenue faster than headcount grows, without the name on the title block paying for it.
triggers: Backlog sits at or near record levels while key licensed roles stay open for months.
Principals are at capacity, with winning work, checking work, and client calls all competing for the same few people.
The firm's distinctive design intelligence is concentrated in a few heads near retirement, and succession is a hope rather than a plan.
Owners and public clients have started asking in RFQs how the firm uses AI, and the current answer is individual improvisation.

evidence.text: Engineering firm leaders surveyed in Q1 2026 reported a median backlog of 11 months, with 47 percent of firms at a year or more and 88 percent still carrying at least one open position.
evidence.source: ACEC Research Institute, Engineering Business Sentiment, Q1 2026 (N=628)
evidence.caveat: A member sentiment survey, not a census; backlog measures demand, not delivery efficiency, and none of it is an AI effect. It frames the capacity problem. It does not prove any solution.

evidence.text: In a preregistered experiment published in Science, access to a general AI assistant reduced time on professional writing tasks by about 40 percent and raised judged quality by about 18 percent (N of about 453).
evidence.caveat: Task-level results on occupation-specific writing, the nearest analog to narratives, reports, and SOQ prose. Not design work, not sealed documents, and not firm-level margin, which is why baselines come before business cases.

evidence.text: The same field experiment that measured large in-frontier gains found professional quality fell when AI was relied on for tasks outside its capability frontier.
evidence.caveat: A consulting field experiment; the transfer to design work is a caution, not a measurement. For a studio, the clearest outside-frontier examples are unverified calculations and code-compliance assertions, which is exactly what the QA/QC gate and responsible charge exist to catch.

pages.headline: One governed platform, instead of another tool on the pile.
pages.outcome: The design technology estate is already crowded: the CAD and BIM environment, the document management system, the specification tool, a decade of project folders on the file server, and now AI in the studios whether it was approved or not. The question on your desk is whether that becomes a platform you can operate and defend, or a sprawl you get blamed for. Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: project-scoped access that mirrors the project team, curated detail and specification libraries as the only corpus retrieval is allowed to reach, provenance that survives into the record set behind a seal, and a sanctioned path good enough that people stop wanting the shadow one.
triggers: Shadow AI is already in the studios, on personal subscriptions and browser tools, and nobody can say which models, drawings, or specifications have passed through them.
Each discipline has procured its own point tool and its own add-ins inside the CAD and BIM environment, every one with a different data posture and none with a shared control model.
Models and documents move to subconsultants and owners through half a dozen channels, so the boundary the firm enforces internally dissolves at the transmittal.
A public owner's security clauses now reach every tool that touches project data, and the estate cannot produce a clean list of which tools those are.

evidence.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023) and its Generative AI Profile (July 2024) give a voluntary, vendor-neutral scaffold for governing AI design, deployment, use, and evaluation.
evidence.caveat: Voluntary frameworks, not mandates and not a professional-liability safe harbor. They have to be adapted to a licensed practice's duty of care, its client contracts, and the responsible-charge rules that govern sealed work.

pages.headline: AI use your firm could defend to an owner, an insurer, or a licensing board.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that the firm uses AI. It is that the firm cannot say how, where, under what controls, and who verified what. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: project-level boundaries, qualified verification at every consequential point, a documented review trail behind every seal, and a disclosure answer ready before anyone asks.
triggers: Owner contracts and public RFQs have started speaking to AI directly, and the firm's posture varies by whoever is asked.
A near-miss surfaced: client project data in an unapproved tool, caught by luck rather than by design.
Accountability for AI-assisted content has never been written into the quality manual, and checkers are assuming someone else verified.
An insurer, auditor, or client questionnaire asked about AI controls and the answer was assembled overnight.

evidence.text: NSPE's Board of Ethical Review concluded in Case 24-2 that AI-assisted drafting can be ethical when a competent engineer thoroughly reviews and verifies the content under the engineer's direction and control, and that uploading client confidential information to an open AI interface without consent is unethical.
evidence.source: NSPE Board of Ethical Review, Case 24-2
evidence.caveat: A hypothetical ethics case interpreting the NSPE Code, not a court decision. Its facts distinguish open interfaces from controlled enterprise systems, client-consent analysis is still required, and it is not legal advice.

pages.headline: An AI investment case built the way you underwrite a fee.
pages.outcome: The fee was underwritten at negotiation, against a scope that was still a sketch, and it gets spent in construction documents where the hours actually live. That asymmetry is the arithmetic any AI case has to survive here: not hours saved in the abstract, but fee protected on projects already priced. The governed version is built accordingly. Baselines before pilots, program cost counted once across the studios that share it, adoption lag priced against the project calendar, ranges instead of points, and freed capacity named to a destination, converted backlog or restored checking capacity, so it shows up as earned value by phase instead of evaporating into utilization.
triggers: AI spend is accumulating studio by studio inside overhead, with no consolidated view of cost and no line connecting it to any project's fee.
A vendor business case reached the principals' table promising hours saved, with no answer for which phase of which project the fee comes back in.
Fee overruns that utilization alone no longer explains, while production hours hide re-solved work.
Write-downs at close keep being explained as rework, and nobody can say what document quality is costing during construction.

aiChanges: The cost side consolidates: one program cost sitting in overhead, counted once, with each workflow carrying only its marginal cost instead of each studio carrying a copy.
The value side gets honest: baselined workflows, deltas measured by phase, and freed hours assigned to converted backlog or restored checking capacity rather than to a slide.
Reporting you can stand behind: every number in the case traces to a source, because in a firm that sells checked work the business case is a work sample.
controls: Baselines captured on named projects before any pilot, so every claim has a before that a project manager would recognize.
One owner and one source of record per metric, with fee and phase figures read from project accounting rather than restated in a deck.
Adoption lag modeled against the project calendar, so value arriving two phases later was planned, not excused.
Ranges with stated assumptions in front of the principals, never false points.
metrics: Program cost, total and per active workflow, read against fee protected on live projects
Fee spent versus phase completed, by project, live
Measured turnaround deltas against baseline on piloted workflows
Backlog months converted to revenue per quarter

evidence.text: Professionals surveyed in 2024 (N=2,205 across legal, tax and accounting, risk and compliance, and C-suite respondents) predicted AI would save them about four hours per week in the near term and twelve within five years. Those figures are expectations respondents reported, not observed savings.
evidence.caveat: A vendor-sponsored global survey of predictions, and design professions were not its focus. Predicted hours may never convert to fee protection or margin; only a baseline and honest measurement can show whether they do.
